title: Put it together: nested loops
idea: TOOL review: consolidate nested loops and interleave earlier tools (single loops, if, counter, len). Thinking-heavy.

exercises.prompt: The big idea of this unit in one line:
options: A loop inside a loop pairs every thing with every other thing
exercises.explanation: Nested loops = each outer item paired with every inner item. Grids, cross-pairings, and comparisons all come from this.

exercises.prompt: Review (single loop): when is ONE loop enough, with no nesting?
options: When you visit each item once, not pairing it with others
exercises.explanation: A single loop handles 'do something to each item' — total, count, max. Nesting is only for pairing or grids. Pick the simpler tool when it fits.
4 outer turns times 5 inner turns = 20 lines. The two ranges multiply — the core counting fact of nesting.

exercises.prompt: Which problems call for NESTED loops? (Pick all.)
options: Compare each player with every other
Add up one list of prices
exercises.explanation: Combinations, pairings, and grids all need nesting. Adding up one list is a single-loop accumulate — no nesting needed.

exercises.prompt: Review (counter): a counter that tallies matching pairs must start at 0 BEFORE both loops.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the counter from earlier laps still starts outside the loops. Inside, it would reset and lose the running tally.

exercises.prompt: Order the code to count pairs that sum to 6 and print the total once.
exercises.explanation: Counter first, nested loops, the sum test, +1 on a match, print once at the end. This weaves nesting, if, and the counter together.

exercises.prompt: Review (len + index): why might you loop with range(len(items)) in a pairing problem?
options: So you can use positions i and j and write 'if i < j' for each pair once
Because you can't loop a list otherwise
len is required for all loops
exercises.explanation: Indexing by position lets 'i < j' select each unordered pair once and skip self-pairs. len() gives the size to range over.
'a < b' keeps each unordered pair once: 0 1, 0 2, 1 2. No self-pairs, no mirror duplicates — a clean three.

exercises.prompt: Review: tracing a small nested loop by hand is the best way to be sure of its output before running a big one.
exercises.explanation: Yes — the hand-trace and hand-example habits from the whole course apply doubly to nesting, where output grows fast.

exercises.prompt: You've finished the nested-loops unit. What new kind of problem can you now solve?
options: 'Each thing against each other thing' — pairs, grids, and combinations
exercises.explanation: Nested loops unlock pairings, grids, and combinations. With read-split-pick (units 85-87) plus this tool, big problems are within reach.
